sections.html:
• Scientific name: Cherax (Astaconephrops) pulcher
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Breeding: medium to difficult
  • KH: 1–6
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: aggressive
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour forms: white, blue and violet, or greenish-grey morph
Cherax pulcher has a very restricted range. It is endemic to Hoa Creek, close to the village of Teminabuan in the south-central part of the Kepala Burung (Vogelkop) Peninsula, West Papua, Indonesia.

These crayfish are found in rivers and streams with moderate to fast flow. In their natural habitat the water has a pH of 6.6, and the natural environment consists of smaller rocks, sand, gravel and many boulders.

A 60-litre tank is the recommended minimum for one Cherax pulcher. Starting with an 80-litre tank per crayfish is better. Reasons for a larger tank:

  • The bigger the tank, the easier it is to set up diverse areas for them to dwell in.
  • Crayfish produce a lot of waste, so it is easier to keep water parameters stable.

Cherax pulcher are great escape artists and will climb air hoses and silicone sealant, so place a fitted lid on the tank. The water line should not be too high.

Make sure the tank is set up correctly and properly cycled. Do a 15–20% water change a week.

Acclimate them carefully and very slowly, as with all invertebrates; 2–3 hours is generally good enough. Be careful with chemicals such as copper: crayfish do not tolerate copper-based medications.

Hiding places are essential, including for moulting; cannibalism after moulting can become a big problem. Cherax pulcher appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, wood, PVC pipes, bricks and similar items, and like spots as narrow as possible to fit into.

• Temperature: 22–26 °C. Temperature is one of the main factors affecting growth, survival and breeding. Higher temperature increases metabolism and breeding rate but reduces lifespan.
  • pH: 6.5–7.5.
  • Hardness: KH above 1 and GH above 4.
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.

Lighting: Cherax pulcher do not really need light as they are nocturnal; adapt lighting to any plants in the tank.

Aeration and water flow: in nature they need high oxygen levels because they live in streams with a swift current, so they appreciate a well-oxygenated tank with decent water flow.

Substrate: they can be kept on any substrate, but smooth gravel is recommended. To keep pH below 7.0, an active substrate that lowers pH is needed, for example ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Fluval Plant and Shrimp Stratum or Akadama bonsai soil.

Plants: they are not plant safe and will eat, cut, shred and uproot everything. Planted tanks are not recommended; the only viable options are plastic plants, floating plants, or cheap plants you are ready to lose.

Cherax pulcher are natural scavengers. In the wild they mainly feed on vegetable debris, roots and stems, supplemented with dead insects, tadpoles, worms and larvae. They are omnivores and can eat almost anything.

In captivity, for best growth they need a good mix of meat and vegetation, with protein at about 20–30% of the diet. Suggested foods:

  • leaves
  • plants
  • vegetables
  • crushed snails
  • earthworms
  • brine shrimp
  • dead fish or shrimp
  • shrimp pellets and granules
  • fish food (e.g. TetraMin flakes)
  • shrimp food (e.g. Hikari crustacean food, algae wafers)
  • frozen bloodworms

Protein-rich foods such as bloodworms and brine shrimp should not be given all the time, only as a treat or in addition to other food.

  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week.
  • Feed before lights out.
  • Leaves and vegetables should be the main food. Oak, Indian almond, walnut leaves and similar should always be available in the tank.
  • Leave food for 24 hours before removing it. Leaves can stay for several days, but remove whatever is not consumed in one day to prevent water contamination.
  • Crayfish often drag food to their hiding spots for later; check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • They need diversity in food, so change the diet periodically.

Calcium plays a huge role for crayfish.

Cherax pulcher are not as aggressive as their bigger cousins (blue crayfish, red crayfish, marbled crayfish, Cherax destructor and others), but they are still not completely peaceful. Like most crayfish they are not social; they are solitary and territorial. They are not usually aggressive towards each other day to day, but when aggression occurs it happens rapidly and without warning.

Males are more aggressive and will likely attack tank mates. One or two may lose a leg or claw, and some fights end badly. They pinch and claw instinctively when threatened.

Do not expect to see much of them. The species is nocturnal and spends most of its time hiding; activity starts at dusk and gradually stops during the night before sunrise. This does not mean they are never seen in the daytime, only that they are less active then. They are very good escape artists, so cover the tank as much as possible.

Tankmates: ideally keep them alone. If several are kept, use one male with 1–2 females, feed them well and provide many hiding places, though aggression cannot be completely avoided. Males are extremely likely to fight when housed together.

Fish: no aggressive fish should be kept with them. Bottom-dwelling and slow-swimming fish are also poor choices. They do not have the ability to kill most fish but will take chunks out of fins. Keeping crayfish with fish is possible but not recommended.

Snails and shrimp: snails and dwarf shrimp can easily become food. Shrimp are usually too fast, but some will still be lost, and any moulting shrimp is an easy meal. Keeping even dwarf crayfish with shrimp is not recommended.

• Males are slightly bigger than females, with much larger claws and narrower tails.
  • Males are more brightly coloured.
  • Look at the lower part of the abdomen (the lower part of the white section of the underbelly). Males have an extra set of pleopods used for internal fertilisation, forming a triangular-ish arrangement of small L-shaped legs. Females have seminal receptacles and lack the extra pleopods found behind the walking legs on males.

There is little information on breeding Cherax pulcher, because the species is rare in the trade rather than because it is difficult. According to a few reports:

  • They mature at about 8–10 months old and approximately 5–6 cm in total length.
  • Females can carry up to 50 eggs. Like all crayfish, females use their appendages to keep the eggs clean and well oxygenated.
  • Eggs hatch in 30–40 days.
  • Adults do not seem particularly aggressive towards the young, but it is still recommended to keep the young in a separate tank with the same water parameters.
  • Compared to adults, tiny crayfish need more protein to grow and can start cannibalising quickly if food is absent.
  • Baby crayfish are very secretive and hide (often burrow) most of the time.

Christian Lukhaup identified Cherax pulcher as a new species of freshwater crayfish in 2015. According to him, it took more than 10 years to find the location because pet shop traders and the local tribes did not want to reveal it. He reported that the tribes associate the crayfish with pregnancy and feared that if he took them, no women would have children again.

Because of its striking colouring, its popularity in the aquarium trade and its use for consumption, the species is declining sharply in the wild. Cherax pulcher is probably the most beautiful crayfish in the hobby, and the species name pulcher means "beautiful" in Latin. It is a hardy crayfish that tolerates a range of water parameters, but being recently discovered, much about it is still unknown.

Appearance: a medium-sized crayfish reaching 10–12 cm. The carapace is often compared to a starry sky or a tropical sunset. Two common colour morphs exist: a white, blue and violet morph with blue and white chelae, and a greenish-grey morph with blue and white chelae. There are 3 spines on the side of the carapace and the eyes are rather large. The front of the carapace is pinkish to striking pink, fading laterally to greenish-grey, and the walking legs are light to dark blue. Life span is up to 4–5 years with proper care.
